metaTitle: Abandoned Checkout Recovery with WhatsApp on Shopify

metaDescription: Use AI to draft Shopify support replies from verified information. Check facts, customer context and promised actions before a colleague sends the answer.
answer: Use AI for Shopify support by giving it verified policy or product information and a narrowly defined writing task, then having a colleague review the draft against the customer’s question. Check live order facts separately. The person sending the reply should verify every promised action, link and exception instead of treating fluent wording as evidence.

Give the reviewer specific facts and promises to check.
Evaluate correction time alongside drafting time saved.
practicalHeading: Turn a return question into a reviewable draft
practicalParagraphs: Hypothetical example: a customer asks whether an opened accessory can be returned. Supply the drafting tool with the approved return conditions and a generalized version of the question. Ask for a short explanation that preserves the opened-item restriction and identifies anything still unknown. Leave names, addresses and unrelated order history out of this writing task.

The reviewer checks the product category, the policy version and the proposed next step. If an exception needs authorization, the reply should explain that review rather than promise acceptance. Keep a simple log of drafting time, review time and factual corrections for the first group of replies. Expand the task only when review remains useful and manageable.

metaTitle: When to Send Review Requests After Product Delivery
metaDescription: Choose a review request delay based on delivery evidence and product use. Test timing with comparable orders and track replies saying the request was early.
answer: Send a product review request after the customer has a reasonable opportunity to receive and use the item. Start from reliable delivery information where available, then choose a delay suited to the product’s learning or usage cycle. Compare similar orders and monitor premature-request replies; there is no single delay that fits every Shopify catalog.
takeaways: Fulfillment and delivery are different scheduling events.
Group products by how long a meaningful experience takes.
Treat “not used it yet” replies as timing feedback.
practicalHeading: Create a product-use timing table
practicalParagraphs: Hypothetical example: group a catalog into a ready-to-use tote and a self-assembly shelf. Begin a timing test from a supported delivery signal and allow the shelf more time because assembly must happen first. Record the chosen delay, the reason for it and how the workflow handles a missing delivery event. These are test choices, not recommended universal waiting periods.

When reviewing results, separate product groups and keep the reporting window consistent. Count eligible orders, invitations, submissions and replies saying the request arrived too soon. If the shelf group needs more time, adjust that group rather than delaying every request. Keep email and WhatsApp invitations on the same schedule so a timing experiment does not accidentally become a frequency experiment.

Review early-request replies before adding reminders.
